Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Bayesian Treed Regressions for Heterogeneous Test-Score Trajectories in Large-Scale Educational Assessments

text.text: In large-scale educational assessments, students' academic outcomes can evolve over time due to various background variables.
For instance, parents' education level, a common moderator, has been found to have time-varying effects on children's test scores, leading to heterogeneous academic trajectories.
To model these varying trajectories, parametric models like hierarchical linear models (HLMs) are commonly deployed.
While these parametric methods are interpretable, their predictive capacities have not been rigorously compared to those of more flexible non-parametric approaches.

We present the results of systematic simulation studies and empirical analyses comparing six parametric specifications to two Bayesian non-parametric methods, Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) and its semi-parametric extension with varying coefficients (VCBART).

Our findings indicate that the BART-based alternatives can (1) achieve out-of-sample prediction close to the best-specified HLM, with standardized out-of-sample errors within 0.002 of the best parametric model in every simulation condition; (2) provide a reasonable amount of interpretability and uncertainty quantification; and (3) run about 20 to 200 times faster than the most saturated parametric model.

This work contributes to the existing literature by demonstrating that Bayesian treed regressions are viable and feasible alternatives to benchmark HLMs for predicting heterogeneous trajectories across time.
In large-scale educational assessments, students' test scores are often heterogeneous at individual levels across time.

Exploring the dynamic nature of students' learning patterns as well as their background characteristics that shape their diverse educational development can offer helpful insights into the efficacy of pedagogical strategies and educational policies.
Typically, we estimate these trajectories with parametric statistical models in which the heterogeneity in test score trajectories is captured by individual-level parameters.
To illustrate, let us consider a simple case where the test scores are a linear function of the time measures.

That is, under the normality assumption, the relationship between test scores and time can be denoted as: where y it and T it are the test scores and time measures for individual i at time t, and σ 2 is the variance of the error term, assumed constant across individuals and occasions throughout this paper.
The coefficients π 0i and π 1i are the intercept and the slope for T it .
We collect the individual-level coefficients in the vector π i = (π 0i , π 1i ) ⊤ , and write π pi for its pth element; the same convention applies once a quadratic term is added later.

To capture the heterogeneous trajectories of test scores, we shall not assume the coefficients π pi to be constants but let them vary with respect to background characteristics, namely, varying coefficients.
This is a common phenomenon in large-scale educational assessments.

For instance, a large body of previous longitudinal studies has shown that children's academic outcomes have time-varying slopes, due to the joint effects of multiple factors at different levels (e.g., Spilt et al., 2012; Ladd and Dinella, 2009; McNeish et al., 2020; Nestler and Humberg, 2022).

text.text: In his "Two Cultures" paper, Breiman (2001) describes two cultures of statistical modeling.
text.formatted: In his "Two Cultures" paper, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Breiman (2001)</ref> describes two cultures of statistical modeling.

text.text: The first culture assumes a data-generating model of a known form and estimates its parameters, which is how the parametric HLMs above operate.
The second culture treats the data-generating process as a black box and approximates it with a flexible algorithm that learns the patterns from the data.
This study compares the two cultures on the prediction of heterogeneous test score trajectories.
The first culture comes with some potential drawbacks.
First and foremost, to attain accurate prediction, the HLMs are supposed to be correctly specified.

This has always been a challenging task as the model should be flexible but rigorous enough to capture the underlying patterns of the data, while being parsimonious enough to avoid overfitting, which means inferences obtained from a specific sample can be generalized to the population or other samples.
In addition, there are a large number of model selection methods that can be considered such as information criteria (e.g., AIC) and regularization methods (e.g., LASSO).

This necessitates researchers to carefully choose appropriate selection methods since different strategies will lead to different final choices of model, which potentially bring in biased statistical inference.

Second, complex hierarchical model structures may fail to converge due to issues such as singularity, as manifested by near zero or negative variances, encountered using frequentist approaches (Snijders and Bosker, 2011; Huang and Anderson, 2021).

text.text: To reiterate, in this study, we first tried to replicate the results of Potter and Roksa (2013) with frequentist HLMs fitted in lme4 (Bates et al., 2015).

text.text: For both outcomes, every model that incorporates moderator effects terminated in a boundary (singular) fit, with the estimated correlations between the random intercept and the random time slopes pushed to the boundary of the parameter space.
Bayesian estimation with proper priors avoids this issue, since the priors keep the variance components away from the boundary.
However, both approaches still require the researcher to specify the model correctly.
Lastly, modeling varying coefficients or heterogeneous time trends can be computationally intense, utilizing a large amount of memory and time.
Given these challenges, we consider Bayesian non-parametric methods that learn the mean function from the data under default priors.
That is, Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) and varying coefficients BART (VCBART).
Essentially, we compare the predictive performance obtained from the hierarchical models, BART, and VCBART through both simulation and empirical studies.

The general goal of this study is to implement an alternative approach that can (1) effectively address these limitations and (2) maintain a comparable level of predictive performance as the benchmark HLMs.

We chose Potter and Roksa (2013)'s work as a starting point to provide a concrete example for the comparisons between baseline HLMs and Bayesian ensemble learning, and our study is not restricted to a single dataset: we employ six simulation conditions and empirical studies with two response variables (reading and math scores).
This work contributes to the existing literature in four aspects.

First, given the complexity of large-scale assessment data, we want to avoid the potential model misspecification issues that are intrinsic to parametric modeling strategies, while maintaining the same level of predictive accuracy as benchmark HLMs; the BART-based methods make minimal parametric assumptions in their default set-up (e.g., Chipman et al., 2010; Hill et al., 2020).

text.text: Second, large-scale data call for robust uncertainty quantification, and we evaluate the calibration of each method's prediction intervals rather than assuming it.

Third, VCBART offers the ability to quantify uncertainty using probabilistic intervals and provides a certain level of interpretability for the effects of the time measures, and we examine its estimated coefficient functions directly.

Lastly, to make the methods easy to use in practice, especially for applied researchers, BART and VCBART are relatively straightforward to implement, and they are more computationally efficient than the saturated parametric models.
The purpose of this paper is not to argue which culture, parametric or non-parametric, is philosophically correct.

Instead, we intend to provide a detailed comparison of benchmark hierarchical parametric models and nonparametric machine learning methods in terms of their predictive performance, when the effects of the time measures vary longitudinally in hierarchical clustered data.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows.
The next section introduces the notation and the pooling concepts used throughout the study.
After that, we formulate the parametric models that will be compared with the BART-based methods, followed by a brief introduction to BART and VCBART.
We then present the simulation studies and the empirical study with the ECLS-K data.
Implications and limitations are discussed at the end of the paper.

text.text: Throughout, bold symbols denote vectors, and X i in particular denotes the vector of moderators for individual i.

This section also introduces the concepts of complete pooling, no pooling, and partial pooling, which are commonly used in Bayesian statistics and are also gaining traction in social science research (Gelman et al., 1995).
text.formatted: This section also introduces the concepts of complete pooling, no pooling, and partial pooling, which are commonly used in Bayesian statistics and are also gaining traction in social science research <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gelman et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Complete pooling ignores the hierarchical clustering structure and treats every observation as part of a single grouping cluster.
For instance, students' test scores can be denoted as y i ∼ N (µ, σ 2 ), where µ is the overall average test score across all schools and σ 2 is the variance.
This approach assumes all the schools' effects are identical, analogous to a regression with only a global intercept and no group-specific parameters.
No pooling treats each group as entirely separate, estimating parameters for each group independently.
That is, student test scores for each school j can be denoted as y ij ∼ N (µ j , σ 2 j ), indicating each school has its own mean and variance.
Unlike the complete pooling model, this allows for different intercepts across groups but ignores the dependency between groups, and no information is shared.
Partial pooling is a compromise between complete pooling and no pooling, allowing information to be shared across groups while still acknowledging group-level differences.
That is, y ij ∼ N (µ j , σ 2 ), µ j ∼ N (µ 0 , τ² ).
In this case, each school has its own mean, but these means center around an overall mean µ 0 with between-school variance τ².
This approach corresponds to the mixed-effects model, where both an overall mean function and group-specific deviations are considered.

Our preference for the pooling notations is due to their flexible hierarchical modeling capabilities, better uncertainty quantification through posterior distributions, and their ability to provide more comprehensive insights for the cluster structure.
With this notation in place, we formulate and refine the models in the next section.
From a General Mean Function to a Centered Quadratic
We reconsider the simple modeling example, function (a), presented in the introduction, which assumes that children's test scores are a linear function of time.

As Figure 1 illustrates, the actual trajectories of test scores are not linear, underscoring the need for a more flexible model that can capture the complex relationships between time measures and test scores.

text.text: We therefore start with a general formulation for predicting test score trajectories at the individual level.

Assuming only that the errors are random and normally distributed, we can write the following model: which indicates that the test scores are a noisy measure of some expected values that depend on T it and the moderators X i .
Without any prior knowledge, however, this function is exceedingly difficult to fit due to several reasons.
First, this is an individual-specific function and thus we need to fit a separate model for each person, which incurs considerable computational burden.
Second, the concrete relationship between y it and {T it , X i } is not clear such that the above function (b) could be linear, non-linear, and possibly involve high-dimensional interactions.
For instance, f i (T it , X i ) may be polynomial, exponential, or even a nonstationary time series function.
Third, with the existence of sparsity, high dimensional interactions in f i (T it , X i ) might bring in issues such as overfitting, collinearity, and computational complexity.

We adopt the quadratic polynomial, the lowest degree that captures the observed curvature, which also keeps the model parsimonious.
A check on the empirical data shows that a cubic term would lower the out-of-sample prediction error by a further three to five percent, so the polynomial degree is itself a specification choice.

text.text: Therefore, instead of employing a general constant mean model, we consider fitting a no-pooling model:
This model places independent priors on each student's coefficients with no shared population mean, so the effects of time measures on test scores for each individual are estimated separately.
Compared to model 1 which assumes every individual has the same trajectory, this model acknowledges individual idiosyncrasies but neglects the dependency between individuals.
The lack of a shared mean has a direct consequence for prediction: a student absent from the training set has no estimated coefficients, and the model predicts that student from the prior alone.
We return to this point when interpreting the out-of-sample results.

For individuals with similar backgrounds, one can instead expect similar progress over time and thus similar trajectories of test scores, a pattern documented in a large body of previous research (e.g., Bassok et al., 2016; Roberts et al., 2010; Buek, 2019; Miller et al., 2020).

In that manner, model 5 is the most saturated model.
This model assumes that individuals with identical moderators will have similar trajectories of test scores.
More specifically, their test scores are noisy measures with the same expected value at specific time points, which vary due to individual idiosyncrasies and different moderator effects.
Based on this highly parametric model, one can understand how the moderators play a role in the trajectories of test scores at an individual level.

Despite its capability for explanation, as we mentioned earlier, there are some potential drawbacks we need to consider before fitting this model: (1) it requires correctly pre-specifying the model; (2) may introduce an overfitting issue; (3) is computationally intense.

Therefore, instead of carefully building these parametric models based on various model selection methods, another useful approach is to apply some black box methods that flexibly approximate f (T it , X i ).

text.text: Generally speaking, BART approximates the unknown f in function (c) by the sum of M independent binary regression trees.

text.text: Starting from the root, each regression tree splits based on the thresholds of the inputs, and the corresponding value at each node is the expected value of the outcome variable, µ i (see Figure 2a).

text.text: In other words, the tree partitions the sample space into several sub-regions (see Figure 2b).

text.text: While a single tree provides a basic partitioning of the sample space, BART takes this concept further by combining multiple such binary trees, each acting as a "weak learner", to create a robust predictive model.
Essentially, BART employs a sum-of-trees approach where each regression tree is intentionally kept shallow by using strong regularizing priors.
This ensemble approach of combining multiple "weak learners" contrasts with those methods relying on a single deep tree that can suffer from instability (Gey and Poggi, 2006).
text.formatted: This ensemble approach of combining multiple "weak learners" contrasts with those methods relying on a single deep tree that can suffer from instability <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gey and Poggi, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Bayesian backfitting MCMC is used to iteratively build these trees.
In each iteration, BART proposes changes to the tree structures including growing and pruning, then updates the terminal node parameters.
These proposals are accepted or rejected based on how well they fit the data, subject to the prior constraints.
This ensemble learning process allows BART to capture complex, non-linear relationships while maintaining computational feasibility and avoiding overfitting.
A more detailed discussion of BART can be found in Chipman et al. (2010) and a review paper by Hill et al. (2020).
text.formatted: A more detailed discussion of BART can be found in <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chipman et al. (2010)</ref> and a review paper by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hill et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: BART and its extensions have been applied to several different domains such as economics and public health (e.g., Prüser, 2019; Scarpone et al., 2020), due to its flexibility in adapting to different data structures as well as its capacity for accurate prediction.

To mimic the real data setting, we consider six conditions by varying the effects of moderators as well as the level of individual random variation.
The six conditions form a 3 × 2 factorial design, crossing the moderator structure (no moderators, mother's education only, or all moderators) with the individual variation (σ p0 = 0 or σ p0 = 0.5);

text.text: To be specific, we generated the data based on the following model: where MOMED denotes mother's education and Z i denotes the remaining moderators.

Each replication generates N = 1,000 students using the moderator values of the first 1,000 students in the empirical data, observed at seven waves (t = 1, 2, . . . , 7), for 7,000 observations in total.
We set β 00 to be 10, β 10 to be 8, and β 20 to be 3 for all six conditions.
These values are chosen based on the coefficients obtained from an ordinary least squares regression fitted to the empirical data.
In the first two conditions, we intend to examine how the parametric methods and BART-based methods differ when there are no moderator effects.
That is, all the β pl and Γ p are set to be zero.
Furthermore, we also want to examine how they perform differently when accounting for individual randomness.
To do so, in the first condition, we let all the σ p0 be zero while in the second condition, we adjust σ p0 to be 0.5.
Therefore, we can regard the second condition as a noisy version of the first condition.
Similarly, in conditions 3 and 4, we introduce a single moderator effect of MOMED on the varying coefficients.
Namely, we let Γ p be zero but assign different values to β pl .
Instead of assuming different levels of mothers' education have a constant effect on the trajectories of students' scores, we release this restriction and allow MOMED to have a diminishing effect.

The diminishing pattern departs from a trend that is linear in the education levels, and its increments are broadly in line with the narrowing gaps between adjacent education levels observed in the empirical data.
For each level of MOMED, we specify β 01 to β 09 as 1, 10, 17, 22, 25, 26, 26.7, 27.2, 27.5, so the increments from the lowest level to the highest level are 9, 7, 5, 3, 1, 0.7, 0.5, and 0.3.
Specifications that treat MOMED as categorical, through indicator variables or tree splits, can represent this pattern, while a linear-in-levels term cannot.
In the same manner, β 1l and β 2l are configured to have diminishing effects on π 1i and π 2i respectively.
Similar to the first two conditions, condition 4 is a noisy version of condition 3 with σ p0 = 0.5.
Finally, we account for all the moderators' effects in conditions 5 and 6.
In particular, Γ p are specified to be non-zero while MOMED has the same diminishing effects as in conditions 3 and 4.
Similarly, condition 6 is the noisy version of condition 5.
Each condition is replicated 100 times with independent draws of the coefficients, the residuals, and the data split.

Within a replication, all methods are fit to the same training set of 900 students (90%) and evaluated on the same held-out set of 100 students (10%); the split is formed at the student level, so every out-of-sample prediction concerns a student entirely absent from the training set.
We fit the six parametric models with the priors described in the previous section after standardizing the outcome.
We chose these priors to match the default settings of VCBART so that we can provide an equitable comparison between the parametric models and the BART-based methods (see Appendix A).

The parametric models are implemented using RStan (Stan Development Team, 2023), with four chains of 2,000 iterations each and the first 1,000 iterations of each chain discarded as warm-up, retaining 4,000 posterior draws.

To compare the predictive performance, we first use the root mean squared error (RMSE), which is a measure of the distance between the actual value y it and the predicted values ˆ︂ y it :
The smaller the RMSE is, the better the prediction is.

Besides RMSE, we also consider using the standardized mean squared errors (SMSE), which is a measure of mean squared errors divided by the mean squared errors between the actual y it and the average response values ȳtrain in the training dataset.
That is, .
SMSE allows us to compare the predictive performances for different types of outcomes.
Similar to RMSE, a lower out-of-sample SMSE indicates a better predictive performance on new data, while a higher value suggests that the model may not generalize well to unseen data.
An SMSE of one corresponds to predicting every observation with the training mean.
To quantify the uncertainty, we use coverage of the 95% prediction intervals, a probability measure that prediction intervals [L, U ] will include the actual values.

As for the computational efficiency, we measured the total time taken (in seconds) to run both the parametric models and the BART-based approaches under the identical sampling conditions described above.
All performance measures are averaged over the 100 replications, and we report Monte Carlo standard errors alongside the means.

The testing set tells a different story.

Model 3 avoids this failure because its hierarchical structure shrinks the individual coefficients toward a common population mean, which gives a sensible prediction for a new student.

In summary, this empirical study has indicated that the BART-based methods achieve out-of-sample prediction comparable to the best parametric model, with BART ahead for reading and model 5 ahead for math.
Together with their computational efficiency, BART-based methods can be a viable alternative to the parametric models, with the caveat of under-coverage for new students noted above.
This study compared the benchmark parametric models and the BART-based methods on the prediction of heterogeneous trajectories of test scores.

Across the six simulation conditions, which crossed the moderator structure with the presence of individual variability, the BART-based methods obtained RMSE and SMSE comparable to the best parametric models.
In the empirical studies, their performance was comparable to the saturated model 5, with BART ahead for reading scores and model 5 ahead for math scores.
The BART-based methods offer several advantages.
They do not require the researcher to pre-specify the model correctly, and their default settings predict well.
They also run much faster than model 5.
VCBART further provides a reasonable degree of interpretability through its estimated coefficient functions.
For large-scale longitudinal studies, we therefore consider the BART-based methods practical alternatives to the standard parametric models.
The results also offer guidance on the choice between the two tree-based methods.
In the simulation conditions with moderator effects, VCBART predicted as accurately as BART or better, and its out-of-sample coverage was higher.
VCBART also returns the estimated coefficient functions, which BART does not.

When the form of the time trend is known, such as the quadratic polynomial in our setting, VCBART provides prediction on par with the best parametric model together with interpretable time coefficients.
BART remains attractive for its shorter computing time and for settings where the form of the time trend itself is uncertain.
A well specified parametric model such as model 5 remains a strong choice in some settings.

It provides direct estimates and credible intervals for the moderator effects Γ p , which the tree-based methods do not, so it suits studies whose goal is formal inference on these effects, and it remained the most accurate method for math scores in our empirical study.
Reaching this accuracy, however, requires several careful steps.
The researcher must choose the form of the time trend, decide which moderators affect which coefficients, include the individual random effects, and check convergence.
Our results show that missing any of these steps costs predictive accuracy, as models 4 and 6 illustrate.
The BART-based methods reach nearly the same accuracy without these steps and at a much lower computational cost.

We therefore suggest the saturated parametric model when formal inference on the moderator effects is needed and the specification can be built with care, and the BART-based methods when prediction is the main goal.
Uncertainty quantification deserves a separate qualification.
The out-of-sample coverage of BART and VCBART fell below the nominal 95% level in the empirical study, by roughly three to nine percentage points depending on the method and outcome.
As implemented here, neither method includes a student-level random effect, so their prediction intervals for a new student omit the between-student variance that the hierarchical models propagate.
Two remedies appear feasible: incorporating a random intercept into the tree model, or calibrating the intervals on a held-out fold.
We leave both for future work.

Regarding prior selection, our strategy was to standardize the outcome and align the priors of the parametric models with the defaults of BART and VCBART, which places comparable shrinkage on all methods (see Appendix A).

For applied researchers we consider this a sensible starting point: the defaults of Chipman et al. (2010) were designed for standardized outcomes, and matching them avoids giving any method an advantage through more diffuse or more concentrated priors.

text.text: There are several limitations of this study which can serve as motivations for future research.
Our analysis is constrained by two primary assumptions that may not be universally applicable.
The first is that we assumed the time measures, the moderators, and the function f are known.
In fields where domain expertise is limited, the roles of these variables might be less clear, possibly necessitating exploratory variable selection techniques.
The second assumption is related to the normality assumption of our data.
In scenarios where data are not normally distributed, employing other prob-ability distributions like Poisson or Bernoulli might be more effective.
In addition, the models operate at the student and occasion levels and do not include a school level.

This choice preserves comparability with Potter and Roksa (2013)  to explore a wider range of analytical tools, and we hope it inspires further methodological development, including computational tools that make these methods more accessible to practitioners in large-scale assessments.

As such, the next step is to learn this function, typically, either through non-parametric approximation or in a parametric manner.
Both of these two types of methods have their pros and cons.
Essentially, non-parametric methods such as BART are flexible and often "off-theshelf", but they are generally difficult to interpret, especially in applied settings.
On the other hand, as mentioned earlier, conventional benchmark parametric models are often interpretable but lack adaptivity and require pre-specifying the models.
In the case of the ECLS-K data, based on Figure1, it is expected that the baseline parametric model would be a polynomial function.
Therefore, considering the (dis)advantages of these two types of methods, our first step is trying to approximate the non-parametric function (c) in a polynomial parametric manner.
and T is the mean of all time points, which is the same for every student because all students are observed at the same seven waves.
That is, T * it denotes the distance between each time point and the average time point.
Centering, rather than any particular expansion, is what reduces the correlation between the linear and quadratic terms and keeps the coefficients interpretable.
The factor of 1/2 on the quadratic term is a scaling convention borrowed from the second-order Taylor polynomial.
A Taylor expansion approximates a smooth function around a chosen point by its value, its slope, and half its second derivative at that point.

Writing the quadratic term as T * 2 it /2 follows this form, so π 1 can be read as the rate of change at the mean time point and π 2 directly as the curvature of the trajectory, without being doubled for interpretation.
The fitted model remains a quadratic polynomial in centered time; the Taylor form only sets the scale of the coefficients.

The coefficients π 0 , π 1 , and π 2 are the regression coefficients for the time measures: π 0 represents the average test score at the mean time point (when T * it = 0); π 1 denotes the rate of change in test scores with respect to time, with larger values indicating more rapid increases or decreases; π 2 describes how the slope π 1 is changing over time.
A positive π 2 suggests accelerating growth, while a negative value indicates accelerating decline.

This approach allows VCBART to capture both the non-linear relationships between moderators and coefficients, and the varying effects of predictors on the outcome.
Unlike BART which approximates the entire function in a non-parametric manner, VCBART only focuses on estimating the varying coefficients with the ensemble of binary regression trees.
In other words, VCBART is a semi-parametric approach with improved interpretability over BART.
For example, VCBART could show how the impact of time (represented by T * it and T * 2 it ) on test scores varies with background variables (i.e., the mother's educational background).

Researchers might find that the rate of change in test scores, π 1 (X i ), is steeper for children whose mothers have higher educational attainment, or that the acceleration of growth, π 2 (X i ), is larger for students from certain educational backgrounds.
These insights can inform more nuanced educational policies and interventions tailored to students based on their family educational backgrounds.

When there are no moderator effects (conditions 1 and 2), all methods except model 2 achieve the same level of predictive accuracy, and their RMSE is close to the residual standard deviation used to generate the data.
In conditions 3 and 4, where MOMED has a diminishing effect on π pi , the RMSE obtained by model 5, VCBART, and BART are very close to one another (0.507, 0.588, and 0.635 in condition 3).
In condition 4, the BART-based methods attain the lowest RMSE (both 1.825), slightly below model 5 (1.844).

As more moderators are incorporated into the true DGP (conditions 5 and 6), model 5 keeps the lowest RMSE in the constant condition (0.505 against 1.264 for VCBART and 1.651 for BART in condition 5), while in the noisy condition 6 VCBART (1.787) is again on par with model 5 (1.846).

Throughout, VCBART stays comparable to the best parametric model and never trails it by more than the gap in condition 5, which is small on the standardized scale: every method that uses the moderators, parametric or tree-based, attains out-of-sample SMSE at or below 0.002 in all conditions.

By contrast, model 4, which omits the individual random errors, reaches RMSE between 6.27 and 6.44 whenever the moderators affect the slopes, and the reference model 6, which lets the moderators shift only the intercept, reaches RMSE between 11.8 and 12.1 (out-of-sample SMSE 0.017 to 0.028).
These gaps show what happens when a parametric model leaves out a term that matters.
Model 6 illustrates the point: Potter and Roksa (2013) preferred this specification, yet it falls well behind the saturated model 5 here.
In summary, based on the RMSE and SMSE results, the BART-based methods perform as well as the best parametric model and clearly outperform the remaining parametric specifications.
The design of the six conditions also lets us examine the effects of the moderators and of the individual variation separately.
Conditions 3 and 5 share the same individual variation (σ p0 = 0) and differ only in the moderators, which grow from MOMED alone to all the moderators.
Across these two conditions, the RMSE of model 5 stays essentially unchanged, while the RMSE of VCBART rises from 0.588 to 1.264 and that of BART from 0.635 to 1.651.
Conditions 3 and 4 share the same moderators and differ only in the individual variation, and the same holds for conditions 5 and 6.
Raising σ p0 from 0 to 0.5 increases the RMSE of every method by a similar amount, because no method can predict the individual random variation of a new student.

While informative, furthermore, our study represents an initial step in comparing BART-based methods with HLMs.
We recognize that more advanced HLM structures exist beyond those examined here.

Further research is needed to assess how BART-based approaches perform against complex HLMs incorporating mixture distributions or latent class structures, as well as other approaches such as growth curve modeling and multilevel structural equation modeling, providing a more complete understanding of their potential in educational data analysis.Building on these findings and limitations, this study offers a detailed comparison of methods and aspires to broaden the methodological perspective in social science research, particularly for those accustomed to conventional parametric approaches for model building.
